items.prompt: A chat app stores 300k messages/s across three self-hosted data centres; clients always fetch 'the last 50 messages of conversation X' and page backwards.
items.why: Write-heavy beyond one node, multi-region, and every read is one partition key plus a range on a sort key → partition by conversation_id, cluster by seq.

items.prompt: A ticketing service must guarantee that a seat is sold at most once and that the order, payment and seat rows change together.
items.why: Multi-row ACID transactions and uniqueness are the deciding signal. Last write wins in a wide-column store can't promise 'sold once'.

items.prompt: A start-up on AWS wants a serverless key + sort-key table for user activity, pays per request, and doesn't want to run any database nodes.
items.why: Same data model as Cassandra, but 'fully managed, no nodes to operate, pay per request' points to the managed service.

items.prompt: A notification service logs every send (~80k/s) with its status, looks entries up by user, newest first, and deletes them after 30 days.
items.why: Append-heavy, keyed by user then ordered by time, with a TTL. Durable disk storage at this volume rules out a memory-only store.

items.prompt: A monitoring system stores CPU samples from 2M hosts every 10 s and needs 5-minute averages over any time range, with heavy compression.
items.why: Numeric samples per series plus compression and downsampling are what a TSDB is for. In Cassandra you'd have to build all of that yourself.

items.prompt: Product managers want to run ad-hoc GROUP BY queries across all events from the last quarter, filtering by any column.
items.why: Ad-hoc filters and aggregates over all rows are the anti-signal for Cassandra, which needs the partition key in every query. A columnar store scans billions of rows quickly.

items.prompt: A live-video platform keeps every comment for replay; popular streams receive millions of comments per hour, so the team buckets partitions by (video_id, hour).
items.why: Time-ordered writes at scale read by key + range, with the partition key bucketed by time to keep partitions bounded: a textbook wide-column model.

items.prompt: A session store must answer in under 1 ms for 500k reads/s; losing a few seconds of sessions on a crash is acceptable.
items.why: Sub-millisecond latency with relaxed durability calls for an in-memory store. Cassandra's disk-backed reads take 1–10 ms.
